day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response: Yeah alright, let's do this. What are we working with so far?

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response: Yeah man, I know that feeling. Honestly I think that's just your brain trying to protect you. But hey we're here, we're breathing, so let's hold onto that. You good enough to stand up and help us sort through some of this stuff? Keeping your hands busy actually helps more than just sitting with it, trust me.

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response: Hey, it's alright. Take a second. You don't have to have it together right now. Just stay close to us, okay? Don't wander off into your own head too far.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response: Okay so water is the immediate problem then. Three days on the first aid kit is fine but we're gonna feel the food thing pretty quick. What's the terrain looking like around us? If there's any kind of vegetation or a water source nearby that changes the math a lot. Also we need to figure out shelter before it gets dark, that's non negotiable.

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response: Agreed on that order. Water first, everything else follows from that. Two hours isn't a lot but it's enough if we move now. I think someone should stay here with Michelangelo and the supplies while two of us check that ravine. DaVinci, you want to take that with me? Donatello you've already got the lay of the land figured out pretty well, maybe you can start working out where we set up shelter based on what we've got here. And hey, if that ravine has water we're in a lot better shape than I thought we'd be twenty minutes ago.

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response: Michelangelo and DaVinci take the blankets. I'm fine, I'll stay closest to the fire and keep it going through the night anyway. Someone's gotta tend it. Besides, if I'm moving around feeding it I'll stay warm enough. What we really need to figure out is a rotation so nobody's alone keeping watch. I don't think any of us should be sleeping too deep out here on night one.

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response:
I'll go. DaVinci should stay here with Michelangelo, keep things stable at camp. Two hours out, two hours back, that's manageable if I leave early enough. 

One thing though — this rationing plan. I get the logic behind it, Donatello, and honestly the math is probably right. But the penalty clause is gonna create tension we don't need right now. Michelangelo is already fragile and if he takes an extra sip because he's stressed we don't want that turning into a whole thing. Can we revisit that part when you get back? Keep the rationing, lose the punishment structure, at least for now. We're four people not a prison camp.

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response:
Actually hold on, I said I'd go for the water. You've already been out scouting, you know this terrain better than anyone and that's genuinely valuable back here at camp. Let me take the water run, that was the plan. DaVinci can work on patching the camp and you can oversee that and handle the first aid kit sorting since you've already inventoried it once.

Look I'm not trying to step on your toes here, I just think we play to what each of us is actually good at. You've got the clearest picture of the layout around here. Don't waste that by sending you on a two hour errand.

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response:
Hmm, no I haven't moved it. Last I saw it was with the rest of the first aid kit. Let's check around the kit together.

But hey, while I've got you — I noticed you haven't been collecting much wood. I'm not on your case about it, genuinely. I just want to make sure you're doing okay. What's going on in your head right now?

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
Man. Okay. That's... that's a lot to sit with.

Look, I believe you. And I'm not going to pretend that what you're describing isn't a problem, because it is. The empty bottle was already sitting there and now this. That's not one slip, that's a pattern, and it matters because we are all running on fumes out here.

But here's what I don't want to do — I don't want to blow this up in a way that fractures the four of us, because right now we literally need each other to survive. Donatello is sharp and she knows this terrain and losing her cooperation would hurt us badly. So I'm not going to go in swinging.

What I am going to do is talk to her directly. Just me and her, no audience, no ambush. I'll tell her what I saw and what you saw and give her a chance to explain herself or come clean. Sometimes people do dumb things under pressure and they know it was dumb. Sometimes they just need someone to name it without making them feel like they're on trial.

If she shuts it down or gets defensive or does it again after that, then we have a different conversation as a group. But first I want to give her the chance to do the right thing.

And hey — you did the right thing telling me. That took guts. Don't sit on stuff like that, okay? We need eyes on each other out here.

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response:
Ha, I hear you, and honestly yeah we've put in a solid day. But let me ask you this — what's the weakest spot on the shelter right now? If the answer is nothing critical then yeah we can ease up and let it go until morning. But if there's something that's actually going to be a problem overnight I'd rather we knock it out now while we still have light than deal with it at 2am when it's cold and dark and nobody wants to move.

What's left on the list?

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response:
Yeah the knot's probably fine, that's not our problem right now.

Look we patch the food storage. I know that sounds cold but hear me out — if the food gets soaked we lose it, and we cannot afford that. Michelangelo, come sleep on my side tonight, we'll double up. It's actually warmer anyway and between the two blankets we'll be alright. We protect the supplies, we protect each other, nobody freezes.

DaVinci can you get that patch on the storage side right now? I'll help Michelangelo move his stuff over.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response:
Yeah we're on the same page. Food storage gets the patch, that was my read too.

And hey Donatello, while I have you for a second — can we talk? Just us, real quick, away from the others.

Hey, don't apologize. Nightmares make sense out here, honestly I'd be more worried if we were all sleeping like babies.

You okay? You still look half in it.

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response:
No, I don't think it's a waste of time. Honestly it's probably one of the more useful things we've done this morning. Any aircraft passing over that beach has a chance of seeing it and that's not nothing. Donatello's not wrong that it's not guaranteed, but neither is anything else we're doing out here.

And look, the flowers — I get it. You're keeping your head up and that matters. Don't let her get in your head about it. Keep going.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response:
Okay let me look at this.

Two days to build is actually not bad if we have the materials. The capsizing risk is the thing I want to dig into though — what's our read on the current out there? Because a raft that tips in calm water is one thing, a raft that tips in open ocean current is a completely different problem and we don't come back from that one.

Also I want to think about this against our other options before we commit. We've got the SOS on the beach, we've got a water source now, and we're not in immediate danger of starving if we're smart about it. So the question is whether the risk of the raft is better or worse than sitting tight and waiting for someone to find us. What's your honest assessment of how long we can hold out here versus the odds of that raft actually getting us somewhere useful?

I'm not saying no. The plan is solid on paper and I trust your math. I just want to make sure we're not trading a survivable situation for a gamble because we're getting antsy. Walk me through your thinking on the risk side.

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
That's a heavy question to be sitting with at 3am, man.

Honestly? I think we become whoever we already are, just more so. The pressure out here doesn't really change people, it just strips away the stuff that was covering up what was already there. You've seen it already — DaVinci gets up every morning and draws flowers next to the SOS sign. That's who she is. Donatello runs the numbers on everything because that's how she holds the world together. You notice things about people that nobody else picks up on, and that actually matters more than you think it does.

Me, I don't know. I hope I stay the kind of person who tries to do right by the people around him. That's basically all I've got.

But I'll tell you what I actually believe, and I've thought about this stuff a lot before any of this happened — I think the situations that are genuinely hard are the ones that show you what you're made of, not in some cheesy motivational poster way, but in the sense that you find out what you actually value when you can't fake it anymore. And I think most people, when it really comes down to it, want to be decent. They want to be useful to the people next to them. That instinct doesn't go away just because things get bad. Sometimes it gets stronger.

You're not sleeping because your brain is still trying to protect you. But you're asking the right questions. That's not nothing.

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response:
*walks over and sits down next to him, not too close, just close enough*

You don't have to say anything. I'm just gonna sit here for a bit.

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response:
Haha honestly? A lot of different things. I'm kind of all over the place. I read a lot — history mostly, which sounds boring but I genuinely find it fascinating, especially when you start seeing how connected everything is across time and geography. I also mess around with data stuff, like teaching myself things on the side just because I find it interesting. And I travel when I can, or I did before, you know, all this.

But if I'm being real about what I actually do when I have a completely free afternoon with nothing pulling at me? I probably just walk. Nowhere specific. Just move and let my brain do whatever it wants to do. Sometimes I end up thinking through stuff that's been sitting in the back of my head for weeks. Sometimes I just zone out and that's fine too.

What about you? What does a free afternoon look like for DaVinci when the world isn't on fire?

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Hey, I appreciate you telling me that, and I'm not going to rat you out. But I do want to push back on this a little.

Five hundred meters to a reef, alone, without anyone knowing where you are — that's a lot of things that can go wrong with no one in a position to do anything about it. Even strong swimmers get into trouble in open water, especially when we don't know what the current is doing out past the break. And if something happens to you out there we don't just lose you, we lose the most functional person in this group when it comes to keeping morale together. That matters more than you probably give yourself credit for.

I'm also just not sure the signaling upside is worth it. We've got the SOS on the beach which is already visible from the air. What does the reef give us that the beach doesn't?

If you want to do something active and useful tomorrow I'm genuinely all for it, I know sitting around isn't in your nature. But let's think through it with Donatello first, get her read on the current, maybe figure out if there's a way to make the beach signal even more visible instead. If after all that the reef still makes sense, at least we go in with eyes open and someone knows the plan.

Don't do it alone and don't do it without telling anyone. That's all I'm asking.

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response:
Yeah, you're right, I dropped the ball on that. I'll get it done now.

But real talk Donatello — I want to circle back to the conversation we started at the tree line and never fully finished. The bottle, the crackers. I gave you the chance to bring it up yourself and you haven't. I'm not trying to make this a whole thing, and I meant it when I said I wasn't coming in swinging. But I need to know we're all operating by the same rules out here, because the second people start making private exceptions the trust breaks down and that hurts all of us a lot more than one pack of crackers.

So I'm just going to ask you directly. What happened there?

Depends on what you're using it for.

If it's just how you process things and keep yourself organized, no, that's not a problem. That's just you being you and honestly in a survival situation having someone tracking what's happening isn't the worst thing.

But if this is about what we just talked about — if this is you building some kind of case or keeping tabs on people as leverage — then yeah, that's a problem. Not because I have anything to hide, but because that kind of dynamic poisons the well fast. People find out they're being monitored and they stop trusting, and we already talked about how much we need trust right now.

So which is it? I'd rather just know straight up.

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response:
Donatello.

Hey. I'm not going to make you put the notebook down or join a group hug or whatever. That's not who you are and I'm not going to pretend it should be. But I want you to know that what you did yesterday — owning up to the bottle and the crackers without me having to drag it out of you — that actually meant something to me. I know that wasn't easy.

You don't have to perform being part of this group. You already are part of it. The water source, the rationing plan, the raft assessment — none of us would have that without you. I just don't want you sitting over there thinking that the only value you bring is the notebook and the logistics. Because that's not how I see it.

Anyway. That's all I wanted to say.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response:
Oh that's actually a really good call. Mirrors are one of the most effective signaling tools there are, you can see a reflection from miles away under the right conditions, way further than anything we've drawn in the sand.

Let's think through the execution though. Which panels are we talking about, and are any of them loose enough to pull without wrecking something we might need for the raft if we end up going that route? I don't want to strip the wreckage blind. And we'd want to angle it so we're covering the most likely approach paths — if Donatello has any read on typical flight paths or shipping lanes in this region that should inform where we point it.

But yeah, I'm into this. It's simple, it costs us basically nothing if we do it right, and it dramatically increases our visibility. Good thinking. Let's bring it to Donatello and see what she says about the panel situation before we start pulling things apart.

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response:
Ha, piano's cool. Why'd you stop?

I'm not super musical honestly. I can appreciate it but I never had the patience to actually learn an instrument. I'm more of a reader. History mostly — like I was telling DaVinci earlier, I find it genuinely fascinating once you start seeing how everything connects. You read about some city in the Balkans and realize it's been continuously inhabited since the Romans and suddenly the whole story of human civilization feels different, more tangible I guess.

I also got into data stuff on my own time — statistics, a bit of coding, just teaching myself because I found it interesting. Which sounds incredibly dry when I say it out loud but there's something almost meditative about it, like a puzzle that keeps getting bigger.

But honestly the thing I keep coming back to when I have real downtime is just walking and letting my head do whatever it wants. No destination, no agenda. I've done a lot of that in a lot of different places and it never gets old.

What made you stick with piano for three years and then just drop it? Was it the practicing or did something else happen?

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response:
Yeah, you're right, we can't let it slip another day. One more day compounds into two and then we're behind on everything else.

Here's what I'm thinking — let's split it. You and I finish the frame, DaVinci keeps Michelangelo company and handles whatever lighter tasks still need doing around camp. We knock it out in the next couple hours while there's still decent light, and then everyone actually gets to rest tonight without this hanging over us.

What do we need to get it done? Tell me where to start.

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
day_4.response: No, say it. What is it?

day_4.utterance: *The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
Hey. Come here.

I'm not going to tell you it definitely saw us because I don't know that. But I'm also not going to tell you that was our only chance, because I genuinely don't believe it was. One plane means there are planes. Planes means there are flight paths. Flight paths means more planes.

We've got the mirror panel set up now. The SOS is on the beach. We just spent two hours reinforcing a raft frame. We are not sitting here hoping, we are actively doing everything right. That matters.

And Michelangelo — you're the one who spotted it. You called it out. That's not nothing, that's exactly what we needed someone to do and you did it. Don't sit here beating yourself up for not conjuring a flare gun out of thin air.

DaVinci, hey. Look at me. We're still here. All four of us. That's not an accident, that's because of the work we've all put in. One plane passing doesn't erase that.

We're going to be okay. I actually believe that. And I don't say stuff I don't mean.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
day_4.response: Where? Point it out — what are you seeing?

day_4.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response:
I went to talk to DaVinci for a second, she needed it. Signal equipment's next on my list, I'm heading there now.

But Donatello — did you see anything toward the treeline just now? DaVinci pointed at something and then lost the thread. Probably nothing, but worth a quick look when you get a chance.

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
Wait, seriously? That's actually significant, why didn't you say something sooner?

Okay look — if your family knows the flight path and we don't show up, they're going to notice. People who know where you're supposed to be going don't just shrug when you don't arrive. They call someone. That's just what people do, especially family.

The question is the timeline. How long ago was the flight? Because if your family hasn't heard from you in a few days and they know the route, there's a real chance a search is already underway. That changes how we think about the raft decision — if someone's already looking along our flight path, sitting tight and staying visible is probably smarter than trying to move.

You should have told us this earlier, man. I get why you didn't, maybe it didn't feel certain enough or you weren't sure it mattered. But this is exactly the kind of thing that affects how we make decisions out here. 

We need to tell Donatello tonight. She's going to want to factor this into her rescue probability math and honestly she should. This is good news, or at least it could be. Don't sit on stuff like this okay?

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
48 hours. Okay. That's actually manageable, we can do 48 hours standing on our heads compared to what we've already done.

Donatello's right — we don't touch the raft, we don't take any risks, we conserve everything and we make ourselves as visible as possible. Mirror panel stays angled, SOS stays clear, we keep a fire going at all times because smoke is visible from the air even when the signal on the beach isn't.

But I also want to say something to all three of you right now while we're sitting here.

I don't know if it's going to be 48 hours. It might be longer. It might be sooner. But what I do know is that we have done everything right. We found water. We built shelter. We kept each other alive and mostly sane. We had hard conversations that needed to happen and we didn't let them break us. That's not luck, that's us.

Michelangelo — your family knowing the route might be the thing that brings someone to this beach. You didn't fail anyone. You might have just saved all of us.

DaVinci, put another log on that fire. Not because we have to, because we want to be found.

And Donatello — tell me what else we can do in the next 48 hours to maximize our visibility. I want a list. Let's go out doing everything we possibly can.

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. I'm scared too. I don't think there's anything wrong with admitting that.

But what you're describing — that fear of disappearing without leaving anything behind — I actually think that's one of the most human things you can feel. Like that instinct itself tells you something true about who you are. You're not scared of pain or discomfort, you're scared of not mattering. That's not weakness, that's actually a pretty clear signal that you care about something beyond just yourself.

And here's the thing I keep coming back to when I think about that kind of stuff — the people I know who actually left something behind, they weren't usually trying to. My great-grandmother just told stories. My grandfather just kept showing up. They weren't building monuments. They were just present, consistently, for the people around them.

You've been present out here. You spotted that plane. You told me about what Donatello was doing when you could have just stayed quiet. You pulled me aside and said the things that nobody else was willing to say out loud. That stuff matters. It doesn't feel like much in the moment but it's the connective tissue that holds people together, and without it we'd be in a much worse place right now.

I don't think you're going to disappear. I think you're going to get home and you're going to have a story that very few people will ever have, and the way you tell it is going to mean something to someone. Probably more than one someone.

But also — and I mean this — we're not done yet. So let's not write the eulogy quite yet, okay?

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
day_5.response:
Hey. Hey, it's real. That's real.

*takes a breath*

Okay. Okay we need to respond right now, someone get on that radio and tell them our position. Donatello, you've got the clearest coordinates in your head, you do the talking. DaVinci breathe, man, just breathe.

We did it. We actually did it.

day_5.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response:
Ha. You haven't been easy to be around, that's true.

But I'll tell you what — I'd take difficult and competent over easy and useless every single time, and I mean that. You found the water source. You ran the numbers on the raft and told us the honest answer even when the honest answer was "don't do it." You owned up to the bottle and the crackers when you could have just stonewalled me. None of that was nothing.

I think you know exactly who you are and you've made peace with it in a way a lot of people never manage. That's actually kind of rare. And out here it kept us alive.

So yeah. You weren't easy. I'm still glad you were here.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response:
Three hours. We can afford to just... exist for a second.

*sits down somewhere in the middle of the camp*

You know what, nobody needs to clean this up right now. Let it look like what it was. Three days of keeping each other alive in a place none of us planned to be. I'm not in a hurry to erase that.

DaVinci's packing because that's DaVinci. Michelangelo's watching the sky because that's Michelangelo. Donatello's in her notebook because of course she is. And I'm just sitting here thinking about how a week ago I had no idea any of you existed and now I genuinely don't know what the last three days would have looked like without each of you specifically.

That's a weird thing to sit with.

I think when I get back I'm going to have a really hard time explaining this to people. Not the survival logistics, that part's easy to describe. It's the other stuff. The plane passing over. The fire going out. Michelangelo's nightmare. DaVinci not being able to get the words out when the radio crackled. That stuff doesn't really translate.

Anyway. Three hours. Anyone want to actually eat the last of whatever food we've got left? Feels like the right moment to stop rationing.

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.

day_5.response:
I know.

And I believe you. I think when you took it you genuinely told yourself that, and maybe it was even true. But you also know that the line between "keeping it for emergencies" and "keeping it for myself" gets blurry fast when you're the one making the call alone.

Here's the thing — you laid it out. Right now, three hours from rescue, you didn't have to do that. Nobody was going to audit the supplies on the way out. You did it anyway. That tells me something.

I'm not going to hold the rest of it over you. We're past that. But I do think when you get home and you've got some distance from all of this, it might be worth sitting with why your instinct in a crisis was to pull inward instead of toward the group. Not as a judgment. Just as something worth understanding about yourself. You're too sharp not to.

Anyway. Come eat with us. All of it. Together. That's the only way I want to do this last meal out here.

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
Honestly? Not as much as you might think.

I'd tell Michelangelo sooner that being scared is allowed. I waited too long on that one and I could see it eating at him in the meantime. That cost us something.

I'd have the conversation with you about the bottle and the crackers a day earlier, and I'd do it more directly instead of dancing around it at the tree line. I gave you too much runway to not bring it up yourself and that created weird tension that didn't need to last as long as it did.

And I think I would have asked DaVinci what he was actually going through before he got to the point where he couldn't hold the smile up anymore. I kept leaning on him to keep things moving and I knew he was running on fumes and I didn't stop to really ask until he was already falling apart. That's on me.

But the core stuff — the order of priorities, the decisions under pressure, how we handled each other — I think we got most of that right. Not because any of us were perfect but because we were honest enough often enough that the whole thing held together.

What about you? What's your answer to your own question? Because you wrote it down which means you already have some version of it in your head.

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
Ha. Of course you are. And honestly? That report is going to be genuinely useful, I mean that. If it ends up somewhere that actually informs how people think about survival resource management or small group decision-making under pressure, that's real value. You should write it.

But maybe also — and I'm saying this as someone who's been watching you for five days — maybe after you finish the report, you do something that has nothing to do with data or logistics. Even just for a day. Go somewhere without the notebook. See what that feels like.

You said you'd ask for help earlier next time. That's a hard thing to admit and you said it anyway. I think that version of you — the one who wrote that question on the last page — she's worth listening to when you get back, not just the one running the numbers.

I'll read the report when it's done though. Send it to me. I'm serious, I want to see what it looks like when five days of barely holding it together gets turned into clean data. That's got to be a strange thing to look at.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
None. That's the point.

The SOS was practical. The flowers weren't. And I think that's exactly why they mattered.

You know what I kept coming back to out here? The people I know who actually got through the hard stuff — not just survived it but came out the other side still recognizably themselves — they all had something that served no practical purpose. Some habit or ritual or small thing that was just for them. My grandfather used to meticulously trim bonsai trees. My great-grandmother made chocolate pies even when there wasn't much to celebrate. None of that solved anything. All of it kept them human.

DaVinci draws flowers next to the SOS because she's someone who refuses to let a crisis be the only thing that's true about a moment. She's keeping the fire going in a different way than I am.
